The ocean does not move from truth, the Vindhya does not grow, O king; a young woman never conceives beyond the proper time.
naradapuran:147:89	Trees stand in truth, showing fruit and flowers; for men the means to the divine and the rest rests on truth, O lord of the earth.
naradapuran:147:90	Truth alone excels a thousand horse-sacrifices; by untruth you are stained by a deed equal to drinking liquor.

A pit is filled with dust and becomes a pit-digger. You gave me your hand in the matter of the boon, O lord of the earth.
naradapuran:149:39	If you transgress that promise of yours and do not keep it, then I shall go, my purpose done, having obtained dharma, yours.
naradapuran:149:40	I am not your dear wife, nor are you my husband, O king. I shall make my own arm my pillow, not in your battle.
naradapuran:149:41	Shame on you, destroyer of dharma, who betrays your own word. Even among mlecchas such a one as you who destroys dharma is not seen.
naradapuran:149:42	I shall abandon you, a very sinner, who have fallen from truth today. Having said so, the fair-hipped one rose quickly,
and as Sati leaving Hara, adorned with divine ornaments, the slender one then set out, accompanied by Brahmins.
Better the touch of liquor than the company of this king; better the touch of a blue garment than of this one fallen from dharma.
Thus Mohini, angry and lamenting loudly, went out of the house with Gautama and others,
crying the words, "Ah, father! Ah, Lord of the world, maker of creation, preservation and end!" — Brahma's mind-born daughter.
Just then Dharmangada, ornament of dharma, mounted on the king of horses, having wandered the whole earth, arrived.
He came before his mother quickly and without envy; those words reached his ears, dear to his father —
words arising from Mohini's mouth and supported by the Brahmins' sayings. Dharmangada, embodiment of dharma, son of Rukmangada, then
dismounted from his horse quickly and went to his father's feet; rising again, he bowed to the best of Brahmins with folded hands.
Then seeing Mohini hurried and angry at heart, perceiving swiftly, he said to his mother with folded hands:
By whom were you insulted, goddess? Why are you angry, beloved of my father? Where are you going now with these best of Brahmins?
Hearing Dharmangada's words Mohini said: "Your father is untruthful, son, by whom the hand was given in vain,
who does so much good, stands with the form of a red ashoka, marked with banner and goad, glorious, generous, golden-armleted:
by your father Rukmangada I cannot stay."
Dharmangada said: "Whatever you say, goddess, I shall do, without doubt. Do not be angry, mother; turn back, beloved of my father."
Mohini said: "With this agreement I was made your father's wife on Mandara, where Shiva stood as witness, the lord of the gods.
Your father, who is adorned with gold, has fallen from the agreement; he does not give me what is due. I consider his growth.
I ask not for gold, grain, elephants, horses, villages or clothes. I ask for that by which he would suffer loss, O king's son.
By what he might satisfy his own body, best of embodied ones — that I begged, son; out of delusion he does not give it.
For the very benefit of his body, son of the king, I asked him, the best of kings, for the sake of happiness.
Today that lord stands in dreadful untruth, equal to drinking liquor.
I would abandon your father, fallen from truth, speaking harsh words, gone from dharma, untrue and deceitful, the lowest; there will be no standing for me with him."
Hearing Mohini's words, the son Dharmangada said: "While I live my father will never be untruthful.
Turn back, fair-hipped one; I shall do what you wish. My father has never said an untruth before, goddess.
How can that king say it now that I am born, in whose truth the worlds with gods, demons and men stand,
by whom the house of Yama was emptied of sinners, whose fame spreads and pervades the circle of the cosmic egg?
How can a king established in false speech be born? How can I trust a king's word unheard, in his absence?
Showing mercy to me, turn back, fair-faced one." Hearing what Dharmangada said, Mohini
turned back, leaning on the king's son's shoulder, to where Rukmangada lay, bright as the sun, as if dead.
She made him lie on the bed, golden, bright with lamp-jewels, painted with coral, excellent,
with legs made of Indra's weapons and jewels, very soft, long and broad, incomparable, charming.
Then with folded hands he said to his father in a gentle voice: "Father, this my mother says that you are untruthful today.
Why will you become untruthful on earth, O king, with your kingdom ruled, with treasury, jewels, elephants, horses and chariots,
bounded by seven oceans? Give her all that you promised her, Lord.
With me holding the bow, father, who will do you wrong? Give the goddess the post of Indra; know that Indra is conquered.
What is hard to get, Brahma's state, stainless, reached by yogis — that too I shall give, having pleased the lotus-born by austerity.
Whatever my mother wishes — in the nether world, on earth, in heaven or in the highest state — I shall give it, conquering gods, men and demons.
I am your servant, O king; sell me, or let me be for a straw; I shall live in the hand of the sinner of tarnished fame as his servant, well fed.
Whatever is hard to do in the three worlds, nothing is ungiveable here, from desire to please; give that also, O king, to the goddess — my life or my mother's life.
By that alone, O king, be endowed with good fame in the world always, outshining multitudes of kings with your own qualities, as rays born of oneself shine in the sky.
If fame is broken, there will be sin, as Manu says is true, in killing subjects. Having cleansed my own spotless fame, how shall I be happy then, O king, able to forgive?"

This very thing she asks: food on Vishnu's day. I shall not give that to Mohini, though asked by gods and demons.
naradapuran:150:13	Let me drink poison, enter fire, fall from a mountain-top, or cut off my own head with a good sword shining like the sky.
naradapuran:150:14	King Rukmangada will not eat on Hari's day on earth. My name 'Rukmangada' is famed in the three worlds,
naradapuran:150:15	and that fame was gathered by me through the Ekadashi fast. How, by eating, shall I destroy my own fame?
naradapuran:150:16	Let it die, or go, or fall, or break into pieces — yet my mind does not turn back, because of Mohini.
naradapuran:150:17	I abandon my own life, with all the people, wives and servants, but I shall never eat food on the holy day of Madhusudana.
...holding her bracelets set with lamp-jewels; ten jewels on each, and fifteen on the necklace;
seven jewels in the parting-ornament, thirteen in the armlet. Thus the girl, set with jewels, bright as gold,
he carried away from the king's palace, the lovely-smiling one, and by the wind's path reached his own abode in a moment.
To that mountain where her husband (the demon) stayed, relying on a belt (?), seeing his cave bright as gold there,
unable to bear his fear, she entered it as he watched — a variegated palace set with many jewels,
filled with many things, with beds and seats, with food, drinking vessels, and eatables and foods of many kinds.
Entering, he put the lotus-eyed one, weeping and terrified, with full hips and breasts, on a bed.
Hearing her weeping, his wife, a she-demon, came quickly to where the demon was.
Seeing her lovely in all limbs, bright as heated gold, the angry she-demon, chaste, rebuked her husband and asked:
Why has this woman been brought, cruel one, while I am alive? You wish for another wife; I am not your wife.
To her thus speaking, the dark-eyed she-demon, her husband the demon said with joy to his own dear lovely-eyed one:

Food has been brought by me for you, auspicious one, from Koshala; another provided by fate stands at the door:
naradapuran:151:93	a Brahmin sleeps, fair-faced one, resting on a sala tree. Bring him quickly, so that I may eat.
Hearing the demon's words, the girl said this: "Demoness, your husband speaks falsely out of fear of you.
Knowing you old, ugly, with a long tongue, he came upon me asleep in my father's house at night, out of desire,
and carried me off, unmarried, weeping, to be his wife." Hearing the princess's words,
she became exceedingly angry, throwing out words; seeing her beauty, she took it to be true.
She thought thus: "She was brought as a wife; surely the demon will drive a nail into my head.
Let no woman in the three worlds be wife of such, who lives pressed by co-wife sorrow.
This is the greatest of all sorrows, without doubt; and sharing a common property would be another trouble."
Thinking so at length, she said to her husband: "The fair-eyed girl brought by you is for me to eat.
I will bring that Brahmin for you to eat, O firm in vows." Then the demon said, "Go, go quickly!"
Blood dripped exceedingly from his mouth, in desire to eat him. Then the dreadful she-demon, hearing her husband's words,
went out with ill hopes and saw the best of Brahmins, endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with jewels of learning.
Seeing him, she took a magic form as a lovely girl of sixteen years, overcome by desire, and approached him.
That broad-hipped one, joined with love, said to the Brahmin: "Who are you, whence have you come, why do you stay here?
I ask: I am a she-demon, longing for a husband, tormented by desire; abandoned by my own husband, I have come to make you my husband."
Hearing her words, my husband, joined with fear, the wise one, taking courage, said to her, auspicious one:
How can a union of demon and man arise, she-demon? Men are held to be food for demons, without doubt.
Hearing that, she said to him again with respect: "What is unthinkable in the world may happen by the connection of fate.
In the Purana this is heard, set in the future Bharata: the she-demon Hidimba, O Brahmin, will be Bhima's wife,
and a son Ghatotkacha will be born of a man, invulnerable to all weapons, who will meet death by a spear.
Therefore do not grieve; by connection of fate I have become your wife, and fate is stronger.
When Shakra had gone to the world of men, and Virochana's son was watching, my husband, a dreadful demon, seized his chance
and took from that house a spear, blazing like a flame of fire. This Vasavi (Indra's) spear is lodged on the sala tree here.
Without being struck by it, O best of Brahmins, a (demon) does not go to Indra; he against whom it is thrown, though immortal, perishes.
Having climbed to the sala-top I shall bring the shining spear and give it into your hand, desiring my husband's death.
If you do not kill the night-ranger with this spear, that fool will devour you and me, without doubt.
He is your great enemy, scorcher of foes, and mine too, who in his folly brought the girl here for a wife.
By my evil-souled husband co-wife rivalry has been created for me; when he is killed, our play will occur."

If I say otherwise, O delighter in love, I would not share in the merit of ghee I have earned.
naradapuran:151:122	The dreadful state that men obtain for Brahmin-slaying, I would reach that state if this is untrue.
naradapuran:151:123	The dreadful state prescribed for a wicked Brahmin who drinks liquor, O Brahmin, I would reach that state.
naradapuran:151:124	The state of a creature attached to his teacher's wife and given to sin, O best of Brahmins — I would obtain that state if I speak falsely.
naradapuran:151:125	The state prescribed by sages for stealing a deposit of gold, seizing land, and killing oneself,
naradapuran:151:126	I follow that state if I say this untrue. The sin of eating meat on the fifth and eighth,
naradapuran:151:127	of intercourse and cutting trees at the waning of the moon, of eating ghee from leavings, of union by day,
naradapuran:151:128	of a householder Brahmin who does not perform the Vaishvadeva, of one who gives no alms to mendicants, of a widow who eats twice,
naradapuran:151:129	of one who eats oil on the sun's transit, goes to a holy place with cows, or bathes in another's pool without lifting clay,
naradapuran:151:130	of one who chews a tooth-twig from a forbidden tree, one bound to a cow (?), one who goes on the heretics' path,
naradapuran:151:131	of one who does worship of ancestors and gods standing on wood or stone, of one who holds a buffalo without cows, who eats from broken bell-metal,
naradapuran:151:132	of one who wears unwashed, torn or another's clothes, who looks at a naked woman, who eats forbidden food,
naradapuran:151:133	the sin, O Brahmin, of one who obstructs the story of Shri Hari — with that sin may I be stained if I speak an untruth to you.
naradapuran:151:134	These sins are named, and also those unnamed, O Brahmin; I would share in all of them if I speak this untruth.
Thus persuaded by her, goddess, my husband, deluded by what was to be, resolved, "So be it."
Without wealth, addicted to vice, defiled by my words, he said to the she-demon the word that gives all success:

Bring that spear quickly; I shall do your word. All this must be given by you to me when the demon is killed.
naradapuran:151:138	In hope of wealth I entered the ocean thick with sea-monsters. Hearing that, the she-demon brought the spear standing on the tree
and gave it for my husband's success, emitting great flames. At that very time the demon, deluded by desire,
was ready to go to the girl; she, frightened, said: "Service of a maiden by a demon is a great sin.
I, daughter of the Kashi king, was taken by you by trick, asleep from my father's house; there is no fault of yours; it had to be so for me.
Now in the middle of this cave the Brahmin will be my saviour. By connection with fate a husband arises; by connection with fate a beloved.
By force of fate come learning, house, happiness, wealth, family; man goes everywhere driven by fate.
Surely, night-ranger, you will be my husband; when a path is laid by fate, what can the wise do?
Therefore bring the Brahmin resting on the sala tree here; ghee, water, kusha, fire — perform the marriage by rule.
Even without kusha, water and fire, a marriage by a Brahmin's word alone is fruitful.
If the Brahmin is not killed by your wife, O demon, then when the homa is done you may eat him."
When the princess said this, the demon, trusting in his heart, went out out of pride,
quickly, overcome by desire, standing outside to bring him.
As he went out, goddess, he himself sneezed, his left eye twitched, and his garment slipped.
Not minding all that, he went out from the mouth of the cave, seeing his wife, bearing a human form, the broad-hipped one,
making a connection, born of wife and husband: "I abandon you, sinful, a cruel-acting demon,
attached to a human woman, polluter of my body." Hearing those dreadful words spoken by his wife, the night-ranger, full of jealousy and anger, ran at her,
raising his arms, opening his mouth wide, going to devour them both, like the wind of time sounding with words that served no purpose.
The Parivettr and Didhishu — Shantanu, Svah-saritpati (Ganga's husband); Didhishu's son, indeed Vasu, who met death by a quarrel over women.
The Kunda and Golaka sons of the Pandavas, born of equal wombs — the praise of them is holy, purifying, destroying sin.
Whom the eternal yoga-embodied Lord is meditated on and remembered directly —
Vishnu attached to a courtesan, the teacher of Prahlada and others, Shri Nrisimha, the slayer of demons, the supreme deity of the gods,
destroyer of the impressions of samsara, the supreme deity of the gods, dweller in the golden-eyed one's house...
Jamadagni's son, himself perfected, whose sin was burned by austerity, Ishvara, doer of the destruction of Kshatriyas, the killing of embryos and similar acts,
himself a bull-like yogi, a Brahmin devoted to teaching the world, who became a cause of the world's censure by acting in accordance with dharma.
Narada, Narada, again and again Narada: Narada devoted to Narayana, Nara, Nara-benefiting, immortal.
Gautama, Gautama, O Brahmin, intent on herding cows, a scholar associated with non-Vedic themes, who nonetheless helped the Veda,
Vasishtha, born of Urvashi, Agastya too, themselves Lords, by whom for the benefit of the world the excellent Vasishtha scripture
was made, in which the Puranas and the Vedas attained likeness; who himself was teacher of Ramachandra, Lord of all;
how was he cursed by Gadhi's son and went to an animal womb? He who subdued the Vindhya, who stood at the ocean as Vatapi,
how was he, giver to the dead (?), approached for the difficult? The Ordainer who is honoured and revered as witness of karma, the grandfather,
how did he, deluded by Mohini, cast off his body? Shiva who is auspicious and gives welfare, directly lord of Nature, higher than the highest,
how did he go to the gods' wives, acting inauspiciously in the cremation ground? Therefore, Brahmin, good conduct is to be followed by rule.
Whoever, filled with the sense of "I", does not abandon... the best of the wise should attain the highest peace, praiseworthy, in both states.
Dharma is held to give liberation; wealth is the one means of dharma. That dharma was accomplished by me with the wealth that is the best of all.
Hear, Brahmin, the subtle course of dharma which I tell: when my husband came, carrying off a maiden,
seeing you in your own duty, he had no fault at all. When I asked him how the girl had been brought,
then he told an untrue word meant for my eating her. Hearing that, she tied me and seeing my bones by herself...
Those who say that in marriage the wife is an obstacle to liberation are not to be known as seers of truth; she is no obstructing wife.
A wife should save her husband falling into hell from sin; the other wife, in the form of the creeper of karma, gives samsara.
